answer: When Mo tried snow ice cream
Use a full stop. Each part makes sense alone, so each is a sentence.
note: Comma splice. Option 2 is a style reason, option 1 and 4 keep the splice.
'sea and ice' would make five things, not four.

Only way to use exactly 8 tiles and get three things: 'tea towels, ice owls and snow globes'. Tiles are not all unique-use (two spare commas), and 'tea' + 'towels' as separate tiles is a trick; solvable but unusual.

answer: Above the station, lights danced across the sky.
It ends the 'where' part, so readers don't see 'lab robots'.
alsoDefensible: 'It stops readers from thinking the lab itself was dancing' is a loose paraphrase of the same idea, though it is a weaker fit than the 'lab robots' misreading.

answer: The 'as soon as' clause ends at 'baton'. The main clause starts after it.
That all the students finished early, and all of them went outside.
Ask 'whose mum?' The wombat answers it, so 'the wombat's mum' is right.

note: Relies on 'All three of them' implying several scientists; 'weeks' and 'The whole town voted' support it but the singular reading is not strictly excluded by text alone.
